criteria.descriptor: Full marks: correctly contrasts independent bi-encoder embedding + vector similarity against a cross-encoder that jointly encodes the pair with cross-attention to produce a score; correctly states the cross-encoder cannot be precomputed/indexed and runs per-pair at query time; the proposed N/k values and two-stage flow are technically sound. Deduct for any incorrect claim (e.g. reranker embeddings stored in Qdrant, reranking boosting recall, cross-encoder run over the whole corpus).

Full marks: addresses all three requested parts (mechanism, concrete pipeline with candidate counts, latency/cost trade-off with tuning) AND names the limitation that reranking cannot recover missed passages. Deduct for each part omitted, for skipping concrete N/k numbers, or for not stating the limitation.

Full marks: explicitly ties the mechanism to the observed symptom (right passage at rank 15-30) and justifies widening N as the fix, and reasons about the recall-vs-latency tension when choosing N rather than asserting a number. Partial credit for correct but shallow justification that states choices without connecting them to the scenario or the trade-off.

Full marks: clear, well-structured answer using correct vocabulary (bi-encoder, cross-encoder, cross-attention, candidate set/N, top-k, two-stage) that a reviewer can follow without rereading. Deduct for vague, disorganised, or jargon-dropping prose that never explains the mechanism.

expected_answer_points: Bi-encoder embeds query and document independently into vectors and scores by cosine/dot-product over precomputed embeddings, so query and document tokens never interact — fine-grained relevance is lost.

Cross-encoder feeds the (query, document) pair jointly through the model with full cross-attention and emits a single relevance score, capturing interactions the bi-encoder cannot, hence more accurate ordering of the same candidates.

Restructure into two stages: use the cheap bi-encoder to retrieve a wider candidate set of N (e.g. 50-100) rather than 5, rerank those N with the cross-encoder, then pass the top k (e.g. 5) to the LLM.
This surfaces the rank-15-30 passage into the final top-5 because the reranker re-scores a larger pool — directly addressing the observed failure.

The cross-encoder cannot precompute or ANN-index document embeddings; it runs one forward pass per (query, doc) pair at query time, so latency and cost scale with N (and it is therefore a second stage, not a whole-corpus first stage).
Tune N to trade recall against the latency budget, and mitigate cost with batching, a distilled/smaller reranker, or a hosted rerank service.
State the limitation: reranking only reorders the retrieved candidates and cannot recover a passage that first-stage retrieval never returned — N and retrieval recall set the ceiling.
common_pitfalls: Claims the cross-encoder produces document embeddings that can be stored/indexed in Qdrant like the bi-encoder's — missing that it scores (query, doc) pairs at query time and cannot be precomputed.
Says reranking will improve recall or surface documents that were never retrieved, confusing reranking (reorders an existing candidate set) with retrieval (bounded by N).
Proposes running the cross-encoder over the whole 400k-chunk corpus, ignoring that it is O(N) forward passes and only viable as a second stage over a small candidate pool.
Describes the cross-encoder as merely 'a bigger/better model' without explaining the joint cross-attention over the pair as the reason it ranks better.
Forgets to widen the first-stage fan-out (still retrieves only 5), so the reranker has nothing new to promote and the fix does nothing.
Ignores the latency/cost consequence of N entirely, or confuses reranking with query rewriting / multi-query fusion.
reference_answer:
(a) Mechanism. The bi-encoder embeds the query and each document independently into fixed vectors; relevance is just a cosine/dot-product between two precomputed points. Because the query and the document never see each other during encoding, fine-grained term interactions (which entity the question is really about, negation, qualifiers) are collapsed into a single vector and often lost — which is exactly why the right passage lands at rank 15-30 instead of the top 5. A cross-encoder instead takes the (query, document) pair *jointly* as one input and runs full self-attention across both, emitting a single relevance score. Because every query token can attend to every document token, it captures the interaction the bi-encoder averages away, so its ordering of the same candidates is far more accurate.

(b) Pipeline. Make it two-stage. Keep the cheap bi-encoder as a first-stage recall net, but widen the fan-out: retrieve top-N candidates (e.g. N=50-100) from Qdrant instead of 5. Feed all N (query, chunk) pairs through the cross-encoder, sort by its score, and pass only the top k=5 to the LLM. LangChain expresses this as a ContextualCompression/rerank step wrapping the base retriever. Now a chunk the bi-encoder ranked 20th can be re-scored into the final top-5.

(c) Trade-off. A cross-encoder cannot precompute or ANN-index document embeddings — it must run one forward pass per (query, chunk) pair at query time, so latency and cost scale linearly with N. Larger N raises recall (more chance the answer is in the pool) but adds reranker calls and latency. Tune N to the latency budget; mitigate with batching, a smaller/distilled reranker, or a hosted rerank API.

Limitation: reranking only reorders the N candidates the first stage returned — it can never surface a passage that retrieval missed. If the answer isn't in the top-N, no reranker recovers it, so N (and chunking/embedding recall) still sets the ceiling.
